items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers analyzing hair and nails from eight Inca children sacrificed about 500 years ago found traces of coca in hair and evidence of alcohol in some children, but none of the hallucinogens they tested for. The remains came from mountain sites in Peru and Argentina and belonged to children aged 6 to 14. The findings suggest the substances may have helped prepare children for the physical and emotional strain of journeys to sacrificial sites rather than induce hallucinations, said archaeologist Dagmara Socha of the University of Warsaw. Harmine, a plant compound associated with Amazonian species, was found in a nail from Juanita, a 14-year-old mummy. The team plans further study of the substances and sacred mountain sites.

items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] Random draw makes Jennifer Thoss Lytton’s mayor after 45-45 tie
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Jennifer Thoss will become mayor of Lytton, British Columbia, after a random draw broke a 45-45 tie with incumbent Denise O’Connor in the Oct. 17 election. A judicial recount at Kamloops Provincial Court on Tuesday confirmed the tally before the draw selected Thoss. Thoss will lead a village rebuilding after a 2021 wildfire that killed two people and destroyed most of its structures. A former councillor, she has criticized the pace of recovery and warned that more than $50 million in planned infrastructure could overwhelm Lytton’s reduced tax base. O’Connor defended the need for recovery staff and infrastructure to attract residents. Thoss said after the draw that she would focus on team-building.

items.title: [space.com] Soviet Union sent Laika into orbit aboard Sputnik 2 with no return plan
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2 with Laika aboard on Nov. 3, 1957, making the Moscow stray the first animal to orbit Earth. The spacecraft had no system to bring her back, and Laika died within hours as the capsule overheated, according to later accounts. The flight came less than a month after Sputnik 1 and aimed to test how a living organism responded to launch and weightlessness. Sensors transmitted Laika’s vital signs to Earth, but Soviet officials initially said she had survived for days. Details of her early death from overheating became public decades later. Sputnik 2 remained in orbit until it burned up on re-entry on April 14, 1958.

items.title: [Fast Company] Jack Dorsey’s Block is cutting jobs again. Here’s what makes these layoffs different
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Jack Dorsey’s fintech company, Block, began a second round of layoffs on Wednesday, months after cutting more than 4,000 jobs in February. The company has not said how many employees are affected at this time. 

The cuts hit the Customer Ops, Risk Ops, and Learning & Content Operations teams supporting Cash App, Block’s consumer financial services app, and Square, its tool for sellers. According to Business Insider, those teams will be “reducing the number of roles, changing some responsibilities, and shifting some reporting lines.” 

Affected employees are expected to receive a “separation package and transition support, similar to those affected in February 2026.” Block has not detailed the new terms. In February, laid-off employees received 20 weeks or more of severance pay, with the final amount dependent on tenure. Their packages also included equity vested until the end of May, six months of healthcare coverage, their company-issued work devices, and an extra $5,000.

Block did not respond to Fast Company’s request for comment as of publication. 

The layoffs came one day after Block reported its third-quarter results on Tuesday. The company said it raised its 2026 gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, up from its initial $12.51 billion estimate. It also projected a fourth-quarter gross profit of $3.32 billion. 

Block hasn’t explained what drove this round of layoffs. Earlier this year, Dorsey announced that the February layoffs were not because of financial issues, but because of “intelligence tools,” like AI.

“A significantly smaller team, using the tools we’re building, can do more and do it better,” Dorsey wrote on X then. “Intelligence tool capabilities are compounding faster every week.”

“We see an opportunity to move faster with smaller, highly talented teams using AI to automate more work,” Block CFO Amrita Ahuja said. 

Block is also continuing to build its own AI products. The company recently released Dessa, a speech-to-speech AI voice model trained on the recording of real human conversations.

items.title: [cloud.google.com] Google bans Chinese partner after backdoor infects 1.3 million Android boxes
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Google and security partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, which had enrolled more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes. Google says it has high confidence that Shenzhen-based manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co. deliberately embedded the backdoor in device firmware and sold criminal groups access to infected hardware. The criminal groups used the devices to commit advertising fraud, route other people’s internet traffic through household connections and install additional malware. Google also reported that operators captured screens, collected account information and system logs, and issued commands remotely. The same malware appeared on telehealth equipment, karaoke machines and digital signs. Google’s takedown targeted XCPE control servers and domains used by more than a dozen related malware families. Google estimates the takedown could also cut criminal access to at least 10 million other devices compromised through separate routes. Videostrong evaded Google’s device checks by loading malicious code after a device’s first boot, Google said. Google has banned Videostrong and its future affiliates from making certified Android devices or supplying software to certified manufacturers, and says it changed its review process. The backdoor remains in affected devices and can reinstall after a reboot. Synthient, a security firm involved in the investigation, recommends disconnecting and replacing affected boxes.

In the United States, forecasts point to warmer-than-average temperatures, wetter conditions in parts of the West and Southwest, and less rain and snow in the Pacific Northwest. California has already seen unusually high coastal water levels; a UC Davis report identifies low-lying roads, airports and neighborhoods at risk of flooding if high tides and winter storms coincide. Former officials and scientists warn that the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has lost roughly one-fifth of its staff since January 2025, weakening its forecasting and response capacity ahead of the season. New Zealand’s outlook for November 2026 through January 2027 points to a greater likelihood of dry conditions in the north and east of the North Island and heavier rain in the south and west of the South Island.

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

🎨 ✏️

Livestock guidance published across the United States, France and Poland focuses on forage stocks, grazing and feed transitions during drought and uneven feed supplies. In France, independent livestock nutrition consultant Eva Garre urged farmers to measure silage and hay reserves, account for losses of 15% to 30% and calculate shortages by date; early maize samples showed starch levels of 18 to 20 points, compared with the usual 34 to 37 in her region. Kenny Simon, an extension forages instructor at the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, recommended rotational grazing, moving hay-feeding sites and planting winter annuals to reduce stress on dry pastures. A Polish cattle farm keeps cows and calves on about 100 hectares of pasture from May through November and produces its own hay and silage. South Dakota State University Extension feedlot specialist Warren Rusche advised keeping newly arrived calves in smaller feedlot pens for their first three weeks and feeding them twice daily during the initial adjustment. Argentine feedlot analyst Andrés Halle cautioned that theoretical feedlot margins can misstate results when current grain prices are applied to grain produced on-farm.

Water access: Wells and movable drinkers between paddocks mean the Polish farm does not need to haul water by tractor each day (topagrar.pl). Pasture planning: Winter forage options cited by the University of Arkansas include ryegrass, wheat, cereal rye, oats and triticale (farms.com). Farm output: The Polish operation produces about 1,500 hay bales and 500 to 600 silage bales annually (topagrar.pl). Feedlot accounting: Argentina’s feedlot occupancy exceeded 2.09 million cattle on Oct. 1, while theoretical calculations showed losses of 80,000 to 160,000 pesos per finished steer (lanueva.com).

Perspective: Eva Garre, independent livestock nutrition consultant: Garre said farmers with limited forage should give the best-quality feed to high-demand animals, including lactating cows and cows being prepared to calve, and use coarser forage for heifers (web-agri.fr). (Web-agri)
Perspective: Warren Rusche, South Dakota State University Extension feedlot specialist: Rusche said early feedlot management should prioritize cattle behavior and rumen adaptation; he advised providing clean, ice-free water and gradually introducing grain and silage (Agweek)
